title: Hidden in a Retaining Wall for Decades: 240-Million-Year-Old Giant Amphibian Finally Named
summary: Sometimes the most extraordinary discoveries are hiding in plain sight—or, in this case, inside a garden retaining wall. A 240-million-year-old fossil, unearthed by a retired chicken farmer in the 1990s, has finally been formally described by paleontologists, and it's shedding new light on a group of ancient amphibians that ruled freshwater habitats long before dinosaurs dominated the land. The farmer had collected rocks from a local quarry to build a wall. One of those stones contained the fossil, which was later donated to the Australian Museum in Sydney. Now, researchers from UNSW Sydney and the museum have named it Arenaerpeton—a temnospondyl, a group of extinct amphibians that lived before and during the age of dinosaurs. 'This fossil is a unique example,' said Lachlan Hart, a PhD candidate at UNSW. 'We don't often find skeletons with the head and body still attached, and the soft tissue preservation is an even rarer occurrence.' The fossil preserves the outline of the creature's skin and robust body, revealing it was far more heavyset than its modern relatives. Superficially, Arenaerpeton resembles a Chinese Giant Salamander, especially in head shape. But its ribs and soft tissue show it was built like a tank. 'It also had some pretty gnarly teeth, including a pair of fang-like tusks on the roof of its mouth,' Hart added. Measuring about 1.2 meters from head to tail, Arenaerpeton was unusually large for its time. It likely preyed on ancient fish like Cleithrolepis in the freshwater systems of the Sydney Basin during the Triassic period. Interestingly, temnospondyls persisted in Australia for another 120 million years, surviving two mass extinctions. Their increasing body size may have been a key survival strategy. Dr. Matthew McCurry, curator of paleontology at the Australian Museum, emphasized the find's importance: 'This is one of the most important fossils found in New South Wales in the past 30 years. It represents a key part of Australia's fossil heritage.' The study appears in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. For a creature that spent decades as part of a wall, Arenaerpeton now stands as a monumental piece of our planet's deep past.
why_it_matters: Discoveries like Arenaerpeton show that important fossils can be found anywhere, even in someone's backyard wall. Understanding these ancient amphibians helps paleontologists piece together how life rebounded after mass extinctions and how today’s amphibians might be related to their giant prehistoric cousins.

background_read: During the Triassic period, about 252–201 million years ago, the supercontinent Pangaea was breaking apart, and the first dinosaurs were just emerging. Freshwater habitats teemed with large amphibians called temnospondyls, which looked like modern salamanders but were often much bigger.

Unlike dinosaurs, temnospondyls survived the mass extinction at the end of the Triassic and persisted for another 120 million years in Australia, adapting by growing larger. The newly named Arenaerpeton was discovered by chance: a retired chicken farmer in New South Wales picked up a fossil-bearing rock from a local quarry and used it in a garden wall.

Decades later, the specimen was donated to the Australian Museum in Sydney. Paleontologists from UNSW Sydney (the University of New South Wales) and the museum formally described the fossil, led by PhD candidate Lachlan Hart. The fossil's rare soft tissue outlines showed it was a heavyset predator with fang-like teeth.
The study, published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, highlights how amateur fossil finds can still make major contributions to science.

perspectives.description: The fossil is exceptionally well preserved, offering rare insights into soft tissue anatomy of early amphibians. It also shows that citizen science and amateur collectors can lead to major scientific breakthroughs.

The fossil was not studied for decades after its discovery, raising concerns about neglected museum collections and the limited resources for paleontology. Many important fossils may still be hidden in construction materials, never to be found.

Temnospondyls were a long-lived group that weathered mass extinctions, much like crocodilians. Their body size increase may be a pattern seen in many surviving lineages after ecological crises, providing a window into evolutionary resilience.

Digital scanning and 3D modeling could reveal even more details from this fossil. The find may encourage people to check their own rock walls and inspire broader searches for overlooked Triassic fossils in Australia, filling gaps in the continent's ancient history.
